concepts.name: Defining Criterion: Liability Creation and Asset Reduction Test
key_dimensions: Core rule: Capital receipt either creates a liability (borrowings) or reduces an asset (disinvestment); revenue receipt does neither
UPSC trap: Grants-in-aid from Centre to States — treated as revenue receipt despite being a transfer, because no liability or asset change occurs
Edge case: Proceeds from sale of physical government assets (e.g., land) — capital receipt despite appearing as 'earnings'
Application: Classifying hybrid instruments like perpetual bonds issued by PSUs

concepts.name: Tax Revenue: Direct vs Indirect Taxes as Revenue Receipts
key_dimensions: All tax revenues are revenue receipts — non-repayable, no asset reduction
Constitutional provisions: Articles 270, 271, 246 — division of tax powers between Union and States
UPSC trap: Surcharges and cesses are NOT shared with states (Article 271) — distinguishing them from basic tax revenue in divisible pool
Recent relevance: Rising share of cess/surcharge in Union tax revenue reducing states' share — fiscal federalism concern

concepts.name: Non-Tax Revenue: Composition and Classification
key_dimensions: Components: Interest receipts on loans given by government, dividends from PSUs, fees, fines, forfeitures, grants from foreign governments
UPSC trap: Interest received by Centre on loans to states is revenue receipt; but the original loan given was a capital expenditure
Distinction: RBI surplus transfer to government — classified as non-tax revenue receipt (dividend/profit transfer), not borrowing
Relevance: Volatility in non-tax revenue due to PSU dividend policy and disinvestment targets affecting fiscal math

concepts.name: Capital Receipts: Borrowings — Domestic and External
key_dimensions: Market borrowings (dated securities, T-bills), small savings, provident funds, external borrowings — all create repayment liability
UPSC trap: Small savings collections routed through NSSF are capital receipts for Centre but create liability to individual depositors
Distinction between gross borrowing and net borrowing (after repayment of principal) — fiscal deficit uses gross borrowing concept
Debt sustainability angle: Rising borrowings increasing interest payments (revenue expenditure) — vicious cycle for fiscal consolidation

concepts.name: Disinvestment Proceeds: Capital Receipt Classification and Controversies
key_dimensions: Disinvestment = sale of government equity in PSUs → reduces government asset → capital receipt
UPSC trap: Using disinvestment proceeds to fund revenue expenditure (subsidies, salaries) is fiscally imprudent — spending capital receipt on revenue account
Strategic disinvestment vs minority stake sale: Both are capital receipts but differ in fiscal and policy implications
National Investment Fund (NIF): Originally created to insulate disinvestment proceeds; later merged with Consolidated Fund — policy reversal angle

concepts.name: Grants vs Loans: The Revenue-Capital Classification Trap
key_dimensions: Grants given by government = revenue expenditure (no repayment expected); Loans given = capital expenditure
Grants received by government = revenue receipt; Loans received = capital receipt
UPSC trap: Grants received from foreign countries or international organisations (World Bank grants) = revenue receipts, NOT capital receipts
Distinction: World Bank loan to India = capital receipt (liability); World Bank grant to India = revenue receipt (no liability)

concepts.name: Revenue Deficit: Meaning, Implications, and FRBM Targets
key_dimensions: Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure − Revenue receipts; indicates government borrowing to meet day-to-day expenses
Normative principle: Revenue account should be in balance or surplus — borrowing only for capital/asset-creating purposes
Effective Revenue Deficit (ERD): Introduced in Union Budget 2011-12; subtracts grants for capital asset creation from revenue deficit
FRBM Act 2003 target: Eliminate revenue deficit; amended targets post-NK Singh Committee — UPSC frequently tests these milestones

concepts.name: Fiscal Deficit: Relationship with Capital and Revenue Receipts
key_dimensions: Fiscal deficit = Total expenditure − Total receipts excluding borrowings; equals net borrowing requirement
UPSC trap: Fiscal deficit is NOT simply revenue deficit + capital deficit; it is the overall financing gap met by borrowings
Fiscal deficit financed by: Market borrowings, small savings, external borrowings, RBI monetisation — all capital receipts
Golden Rule of fiscal policy: Fiscal deficit should not exceed capital expenditure (borrowing only to invest, not consume)

concepts.name: Primary Deficit: Isolating Debt Sustainability from Interest Burden
key_dimensions: Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit − Net interest payments; shows deficit excluding inherited debt service cost
Significance: A zero primary deficit means current revenue is sufficient for current non-interest expenditure — debt stabilising condition
UPSC trap: Interest payments are revenue expenditure but are subtracted from fiscal deficit to get primary deficit — conceptual overlap
India context: Years when primary deficit was near zero vs fiscal deficit remained high — demonstrates legacy debt burden

concepts.name: Capital Budget vs Revenue Budget: Structural Distinction
key_dimensions: Revenue Budget: Revenue receipts + Revenue expenditure; Capital Budget: Capital receipts + Capital expenditure
UPSC trap: The two budgets are presented together in Union Budget but conceptually distinct — Article 112 requires Annual Financial Statement
Consolidated Fund of India receives both revenue and capital receipts — single fund but analytically bifurcated
Implication: A surplus revenue budget can finance part of capital expenditure — concept of 'revenue surplus financing capex'

concepts.name: Monetisation of Deficit: Capital Receipt with Inflationary Implications
key_dimensions: Borrowing from RBI (Ways and Means Advances, Ad-hoc T-bills historically) = capital receipt but creates high-powered money
Fiscal Responsibility: FRBM Act prohibits direct RBI subscription to primary government securities — ended automatic monetisation
UPSC trap: RBI buying government bonds in secondary market (Open Market Operations) is monetary policy, NOT direct monetisation
COVID context: Debate on temporary suspension of FRBM and quasi-monetisation through special OMOs (Operation Twist)

concepts.name: Receipts from Recovery of Loans: Capital Receipt Classification
key_dimensions: When Centre recovers loans given to states/PSUs — principal repayment received = capital receipt (asset conversion, not creation of liability)
UPSC trap: Interest received on these loans = revenue receipt; principal recovered = capital receipt — same transaction, dual classification
Significance in budget arithmetic: Declining loan recoveries reduce capital receipts, worsening fiscal deficit without affecting revenue deficit
Historical context: Pre-2000s large Central loans to states replaced by devolution/grants — structural shift in capital receipts composition

concepts.name: FRBM Act 2003 and NK Singh Committee: Fiscal Rules Governing Receipt-Expenditure Balance
key_dimensions: Original FRBM targets: Eliminate revenue deficit, reduce fiscal deficit to 3% of GDP by 2008-09 — subsequently missed and revised
NK Singh Committee (2017): Recommended fiscal deficit target of 3% by 2020, revenue deficit of 0.8%, debt-to-GDP target of 60%
Escape clause: FRBM allows deviation up to 0.5% of GDP for national security, calamity — invoked during COVID-19
UPSC trap: FRBM covers Central government; states have their own fiscal responsibility legislation — not a uniform national framework

concepts.name: Cess and Surcharge: Revenue Receipt Anomaly in Federal Finance
key_dimensions: Cess and surcharge are tax revenues (revenue receipts) but constitutionally excluded from the divisible pool under Article 271
UPSC trap: States receive NO share of cess/surcharge — this is a deliberate constitutional design, not an administrative decision
Fiscal implication: Rising cess (Health & Education Cess, Swachh Bharat Cess) increases Centre's revenue without increasing state transfers
GST Compensation Cess: Sui generis — collected as cess, kept in separate fund, transferred to states — exception to general cess rule

concepts.name: External Grants vs External Loans: Receipt Classification in External Aid
key_dimensions: External loan (bilateral/multilateral) = capital receipt (creates repayment liability in foreign currency)
External grant = revenue receipt (no repayment liability) — UPSC frequently tests this counterintuitive classification
Currency risk dimension: External loans create foreign exchange liability — relevant to debt sustainability and CAD analysis
Concessional loans (ODA): Low-interest external borrowings are still capital receipts despite grant-like terms — classification based on repayability, not interest rate

concepts.name: Public Account of India: Receipts Outside Consolidated Fund
key_dimensions: Public Account receipts (PPF, small savings, provident funds) are NOT government's own money — held in trust/fiduciary capacity
UPSC trap: Small savings in Public Account are capital receipts for the government when used for financing fiscal deficit, but are liabilities
Distinction: Consolidated Fund receipts (tax, non-tax, borrowings) vs Public Account receipts (provident funds, deposits) — Parliamentary control differs
National Small Savings Fund (NSSF): Receipts from small savings — used to finance Centre and State deficits — capital receipt nature

concepts.name: Spectrum Auction and Licence Fee Proceeds: Capital or Revenue Receipt Debate
key_dimensions: UPSC trap: Spectrum auction proceeds — classified as capital receipts (sale of asset/right), NOT revenue receipts, though recurring
Licence fees paid annually by telecom companies = revenue receipts (periodic fee, no asset transfer)
One-time spectrum assignment fee = capital receipt; annual spectrum usage charge = revenue receipt — same sector, dual classification
Fiscal implication: Treating one-time capital receipts as regular revenue inflates apparent fiscal health — window dressing concern

concepts.name: Asset Monetisation Pipeline: Capital Receipts Innovation
key_dimensions: National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP, 2021): Leasing brownfield government assets to private sector — generates capital receipts without ownership transfer
Classification nuance: Upfront lease premium received = capital receipt; annual concession fee = revenue receipt
UPSC trap: Monetisation ≠ privatisation — government retains ownership; asset returns after lease period — not a permanent asset reduction
Fiscal use of proceeds: NMP proceeds to fund new infrastructure (capital expenditure) — fiscally appropriate use of capital receipts

concepts.name: Goods and Services Tax (GST) Revenue: Federal Dimension of Revenue Receipts
key_dimensions: CGST = Central revenue receipt; SGST = State revenue receipt; IGST = Central receipt, subsequently apportioned to states
UPSC trap: GST Compensation to states (pre-June 2022) came from GST Compensation Cess — a capital-like transfer, not from consolidated tax pool
Integrated treatment: IGST collected by Centre but not Centre's own revenue — fiduciary nature similar to Public Account
Buoyancy of GST revenue: Tax buoyancy > 1 means GST grows faster than GDP — positive signal for both Centre and State revenue receipts

concepts.name: Off-Budget Borrowings: Hidden Capital Receipts and Fiscal Transparency
key_dimensions: Off-budget borrowings: Government directs PSUs/FCI/NHAI to borrow on its behalf — does NOT appear as capital receipt in Union Budget
CAG and Parliamentary Standing Committee criticism: Off-budget borrowings understate true fiscal deficit — fiscal opacity concern
Examples: FCI borrowings from NSSF for food subsidy, NHAI borrowings for road construction shown off-budget
UPSC trap: These borrowings are economically government debt (liability) but not classified as capital receipts in budget — distinction between economic and accounting treatment
